title: "Bitmask"
description: "Learn Bitmask with a complete numerical recurrence, proof, counterexample and small tested implementation."
---

## One problem you can understand by hand

**LeetCode 698 — Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets.** A subset of available items must be represented as part of a DP state. Storing the list of chosen elements in every key is cumbersome.

A good algorithm explanation begins with the decision you need to make, not the method's name. Write down the smallest example and the exact choice available at each step.

## The approach that looks convincing but fails

Use long strings or sorted copies to identify the same subset repeatedly. A set of n choices has exactly 2^n possibilities, but representations should be compact.

Do not improve the code yet. Ask whether the information you need is already present in a smaller version of the same problem.

## The key reasoning step

Use one bit per item index: a 1 means 'already chosen' and 0 means 'available'. Repeated values at different indices still receive different bits.

## From actual numbers to mathematics

$$
mask(S)=\sum_{i\in S}2^i
$$

**What every symbol means:** S is a set of chosen ZERO-BASED indices, i is an item index, 2^i is the binary place value for that index, and mask(S) is the integer encoding the subset.

**Now substitute numbers into that same relationship:** For items at positions {0,2,3}, mask=2⁰+2²+2³=1+4+8=13, whose binary representation is 1101. It marks items 0,2,3 as chosen and item 1 as absent. Testing bit 2 uses (13 & 4) ≠ 0.

If a recurrence contains two alternatives, identify which real-world decision each alternative represents. If the formula uses a maximum, say what is being maximised and why the alternatives cover all legal choices.

## Why the result is actually correct

Binary positional representation is unique. Each bit carries one independent yes/no choice, so no two distinct subsets of fixed indices share the same mask.

A complete proof needs an initial state/base case, preservation of the hypothesis and an explanation that no valid possibility has been missed.

## Actual implementation

The [original, tested JavaScript implementation](../examples/patterns.mjs) exports `subsets`:

~~~js
import { subsets } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(subsets([1,2,3]));
~~~

Run this from a `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The same function is exercised by [the unit tests](../examples/patterns.test.mjs). The implementation is intentionally tiny so the recurrence remains visible.

## Complexity and failure conditions

**Cost model:** O(1) bit operations for fixed-width masks; a full subset DP has up to O(2^n) states, n being item count.

**A classic mistake:** Bitmask tricks rely on finite integer width. JavaScript bitwise operations convert to signed 32-bit integers, so a plain (1 << i) is unsafe for arbitrary i≥31; use BigInt for wider masks.

In interviews, identifying **why a tempting shortcut fails** is more valuable than memorising one template. For example, a greedy choice needs an exchange proof; if no such proof exists, dynamic programming may be necessary.

## Try teaching it back

Use only the numbers in the worked example and explain the state, choices, update, stopping condition, and why no better answer is excluded. Then change one assumption and explain what changes.
